paragraphs.source_en: > My own total portfolio holds about 50/50 indexed stocks and bonds, largely indexed short- and intermediate-term. At my age of 88, I’m comfortable with that allocation. But I confess that half of the time I worry that I have too much in equities, and the other half of the time that I don’t have enough in equities. Finally, we’re all just human beings, operating in a fog of ignorance and relying on our circumstances and our common sense to establish an appropriate asset allocation.

paragraphs.source_en: # Chapter Nineteen Asset Allocation II: *Retirement Investing, and Funds That Set Your Asset Allocation in Advance.*

units.source_en: # Chapter Nineteen Asset Allocation II: *Retirement Investing, and Funds That Set Your Asset Allocation in Advance.*

paragraphs.source_en: IN MY 1993 BOOK *Bogle on Mutual Funds*, after discussing the large number of asset allocation strategies available to investors, I raised the possibility that “less is more”—that a simple mainstream (i.e., index) balanced fund, 60 percent in U.S. stocks, 40 percent in U.S. bonds, one that provides extraordinary diversification and operates at rock-bottom cost, would offer the functional equivalent of having your entire portfolio overseen by an investment advisory firm.
